Antonín Dvořák. The Czech composer who integrated Czech and Slavic folk rhythms into Classical structures and became a leading figure of musical nationalism in the nineteenth century.

His most recognizable works are the Slavonic Dances, which launched his career with their inspiration from traditional Czech dances like the furiant and dumka. He also wrote the folklore-inspired opera Rusalka, which remains famous especially for the soprano aria Song to the Moon, where the water nymph Rusalka asks the moon to tell a human prince of her love.

In 1892, Dvořák traveled to the United States to serve as the director of the National Conservatory of Music of America in New York City. During his American stay, he was deeply inspired by African-American spirituals and Native American music. This led him to compose his most famous work, the New World Symphony.

The symphony was composed in New York in 1893 with the subtitle From the New World. It weaves together melodies inspired by African-American spirituals such as Swing Low, Sweet Chariot and Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's epic poem The Song of Hiawatha. The second movement, the Largo, features a famous nostalgic solo for the English horn. This movement was later set to lyrics by William Arms Fisher as the song Goin' Home.

During his American period, he also composed the American String Quartet, String Quartet No. 12 in F major, in just three days during a summer holiday in the Czech-immigrant community of Spillville, Iowa.

His Cello Concerto in B minor is widely considered the greatest concerto for the instrument. Written in America, it incorporates a melody from his own song Lasst mich allein, meaning Leave me alone, composed to mourn the terminal illness of his sister-in-law Josefina.

Brahms was Dvořák's close friend and influential advocate, introducing him to his publisher Simrock and correcting his proofs. His travels across the American heartland exposed him to the scale and folk music of the American frontier.
